teachers.sum: One of the earliest church leaders after the apostles, Clement wrote a letter to the divided church in Corinth (1 Clement, c. AD 96) urging humility, order, and love. His letter is among the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament and shows how the first generation after the apostles applied their teaching.
ideas: Unity and humility in the local church
Respect for church order and leadership
The resurrection as the ground of Christian hope
teachers.img: Clement of Rome, an elderly first-century bishop in simple Roman tunic and cloak, dictating a letter by oil lamp in a Roman house church

q.q: Let us fix our gaze on the blood of Christ, and know that it is precious to His Father, because it was poured out for our salvation.

teachers.sum: Bishop of Antioch condemned to death in Rome, Ignatius wrote seven letters while traveling to his execution. They breathe fearless devotion to Christ, warn against false teaching that denied Jesus truly came in the flesh, and urge believers to stay united around their leaders.
ideas: Christ truly God and truly man against early denials
Unity of the church around its shepherd
Martyrdom as faithful witness
works: Seven Letters (to the Ephesians, Romans, Smyrnaeans, and others)
teachers.img: Ignatius of Antioch, a resolute second-century bishop in chains escorted by Roman soldiers along a stone road, writing letters at a rest stop

q.q: I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.

teachers.sum: Led by James the brother of Jesus and the apostles, the first council in church history resolved the debate over whether Gentile converts had to follow the Mosaic law and be circumcised. It was decided that Gentiles are saved by grace through faith in Christ alone and need not undergo circumcision, though they were asked to abstain from blood, strangled meat, food offered to idols, and sexual immorality to preserve fellowship with Jewish believers. This decision fundamentally shaped Christian identity as distinct from Judaism, establishing a global, multi-ethnic church.
ideas: Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone for both Jews and Gentiles
Gentiles are free from the ceremonial requirements of the Mosaic Law, including circumcision
Pastoral sensitivity and compromise preserve unity and fellowship in a diverse church

Reformed Perspective: Endorsed as the biblical foundation for representative church government (synods) and the doctrine of justification by faith alone. The temporary restrictions are viewed as laws of love for unity, not permanent salvific conditions.
teachers.img: The Council of Jerusalem: James the brother of Jesus standing in a simple first-century stone meeting hall, gesturing warmly, as the apostles Peter, Paul, and Barnabas listen intently among gathered elders

teachers.trad: Apostolic Father, disciple of the apostle John
teachers.sum: A personal disciple of the apostle John, Polycarp linked the apostolic age to the next generations. Martyred at age 86, his famous words at the stake — 'Eighty-six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong' — became a model of faithfulness to the end.
ideas: Faithful endurance under persecution
Guarding the apostles' teaching
A living link from the apostles to the early church
teachers.img: Polycarp, a white-bearded elderly bishop standing serene before a Roman arena crowd, hands unbound beside an unlit pyre

q.q: Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?

teachers.sum: A trained philosopher who found in Christ the true philosophy, Justin wrote the first great defenses (apologies) of Christianity to the Roman world. His writings preserve the earliest detailed description of Christian worship — Scripture reading, preaching, prayer, and the Lord's Supper on the Lord's Day.
ideas: Defending the faith with reason toward outsiders
Christ as the true Word (Logos) all truth points to
Earliest window into early Christian worship
teachers.img: Justin Martyr, a second-century philosopher in a scholar's pallium cloak, reasoning from scrolls in a Roman colonnade

q.q: We who formerly hated and destroyed one another now live together and pray for our enemies.

teachers.sum: Taught by Polycarp, Irenaeus answered the Gnostic sects that claimed secret knowledge and rejected the Creator God. He grounded the faith in the public teaching of the apostles handed down in the churches, championed the unity of Old and New Testaments, and taught that in Christ, God 'recapitulated' — summed up and healed — the human story Adam broke.
ideas: Scripture's one storyline from creation to Christ
Apostolic teaching as public, not secret
Christ the second Adam who sums up and restores humanity
teachers.img: Irenaeus of Lyons, a second-century bishop at a writing desk stacked with codices, Gallic hills through a window

q.q: The glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God.

teachers.sum: A fiery Carthaginian lawyer-turned-theologian, Tertullian gave the Latin church its theological vocabulary — he coined the term 'Trinity' (trinitas) for the one God in three persons. His defenses of Christians under persecution produced the famous line that the blood of the martyrs is seed.
ideas: Coined 'Trinity': one substance, three persons
Bold public defense of persecuted believers
Holiness and seriousness in Christian living
teachers.img: Tertullian, an intense North African advocate in Roman dress, mid-argument at a desk of legal scrolls in Carthage

q.q: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.

teachers.sum: The most prolific scholar of the early church, Origen produced the Hexapla — a massive six-column comparison of Old Testament texts — and preached through most of the Bible. He pioneered careful verse-by-verse commentary, though some of his speculative ideas were later judged to go beyond Scripture, a reminder that even brilliant teachers must be tested by the text.
ideas: Verse-by-verse biblical scholarship
Comparing manuscripts to establish the text
The need to test every teacher against Scripture
works: Commentaries and homilies on most biblical books
teachers.img: Origen, a lean third-century scholar surrounded by shelves of scrolls in the great library district of Alexandria, comparing manuscript columns by lamplight

q.q: The Scriptures were written by the Spirit of God, and have a meaning not only such as is apparent at first sight, but also another which escapes the notice of most.

teachers.trad: Bishop, defender of Christ's full deity
teachers.sum: When the Arian teaching swept the empire claiming the Son was a created being, Athanasius stood nearly alone — exiled five times — insisting that only God can save, so the Christ who saves must be fully God. His Easter letter of AD 367 also contains the earliest list matching our 27 New Testament books.
ideas: Christ fully God, of one being with the Father (Nicaea)
Salvation itself hangs on who Christ is
Earliest complete New Testament canon list
teachers.img: Athanasius, a small dark-skinned Egyptian bishop with piercing eyes, standing firm before imperial officials in a basilica hall

q.q: He was made man that we might be made partakers of the divine nature.

teachers.sum: Called by Emperor Constantine, the council defended the full deity of Christ against the teachings of Arius, who claimed the Son was a created being. The council declared that Jesus Christ is 'homoousios' (of the same substance/being) with the Father, eternally begotten and not made. This established the bedrock of Trinitarian orthodoxy and resulted in the original Nicene Creed, permanently shaping the church's understanding of Jesus as truly God.
ideas: Jesus Christ is fully God, of one substance (homoousios) with the Father
Condemnation of Arianism as a sub-biblical heresy that denies Christ's eternal deity
Formulation of the original Nicene Creed as the baseline definition of Christian faith

Reformed Perspective: Fully accepts Nicene orthodoxy on Christ's deity as a faithful summary of Scripture, while affirming that the council's authority is subordinate to the written Word of God (Sola Scriptura).
teachers.img: The First Council of Nicaea: A vast, brightly lit Roman hall in AD 325, where a multitude of early bishops gather around an open scroll of Scripture as Emperor Constantine looks on

teachers.sum: Bishop of Caesarea and eldest of the Cappadocian Fathers, Basil defended the deity of the Holy Spirit and organized massive care for the poor — his 'Basiliad' complex of hospitals and hostels was called a new city. He showed that right doctrine and radical mercy belong together.
ideas: The Holy Spirit is fully God and to be worshiped
Care for the poor as essential Christian practice
Ordered community life devoted to prayer and work
teachers.img: Basil the Great, a gaunt bearded bishop in dark robes directing food distribution to the poor outside a great charitable complex in Cappadocia

teachers.sum: A reluctant, poetic bishop whose Five Theological Orations in Constantinople gave the church its clearest early language for the Trinity — one God in three co-equal persons. His axiom about the incarnation, 'what has not been assumed has not been healed,' safeguarded that Christ took on full humanity to save the whole person.
ideas: Precise, worshipful Trinitarian language
Christ assumed full humanity to heal all of it
Theology done in a spirit of prayer
teachers.img: Gregory of Nazianzus, a contemplative bearded bishop preaching by candlelight in a small chapel in Constantinople, listeners pressed close

teachers.sum: Basil's younger brother and the most philosophical of the Cappadocians, Gregory defended the Trinity against its critics and wrote movingly on the endless journey of knowing the infinite God. He was also one of the first Christian voices to argue against slavery as an institution.
ideas: The infinite God known in ever-deepening pursuit
Complete equality of the three divine persons
Early Christian critique of slavery
teachers.img: Gregory of Nyssa, a thoughtful fourth-century bishop walking a mountain path at dawn in Cappadocia, symbolizing the soul's endless ascent

teachers.sum: A Roman governor acclaimed bishop by the crowd before he was even baptized, Ambrose became a fearless shepherd who barred an emperor from communion until he repented of a massacre — church conscience standing above state power. His preaching was instrumental in Augustine's conversion, and his hymns shaped Western worship.
ideas: The church's moral independence from the state
Rulers stand under God's law like everyone else
Hymn-singing as congregational worship
works: On the Duties of the Clergy
teachers.img: Ambrose of Milan, a stately bishop in white standing at the basilica door, gently but firmly barring an armored Roman emperor

teachers.sum: The greatest preacher of the early church — nicknamed 'Golden-Mouth' — John expounded Scripture verse by verse to packed congregations in Antioch and Constantinople, applying it fearlessly to wealth, power, and daily life. His boldness toward the imperial court cost him his office and finally his life in exile.
ideas: Expository preaching through whole books
Scripture applied to money, power, and the poor
Courage before corrupt power
works: Homilies on Matthew, John, Romans, and many other books
teachers.img: John Chrysostom, a slight ascetic preacher with blazing eyes in a pulpit above a vast rapt congregation in a Constantinople basilica

q.q: The ignorance of Scripture is the cause of all evils.

teachers.sum: An irascible genius of languages, Jerome moved to a cave-study in Bethlehem and translated the Bible into Latin directly from Hebrew and Greek — the Vulgate, which served the Western church for a thousand years. His maxim endures: 'Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.'
ideas: Translation from the original Hebrew and Greek
The Bible in the language of the people of its day
Rigorous scholarship in service of the church
teachers.img: Jerome, a weathered scholar in a lamplit stone study in Bethlehem, Hebrew and Greek manuscripts spread around his Latin translation work

q.q: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

teachers.sum: Converted from a restless life after hearing a child chant 'take up and read' (Romans 13), Augustine became the towering theologian of the West. Against Pelagius he taught that salvation is by grace alone because sin runs deeper than willpower; his Confessions invented the spiritual autobiography, and The City of God reframed history around God's kingdom rather than Rome's.
ideas: Salvation by grace, not human effort
Original sin: the heart's deep bent needs rescue
'Our hearts are restless until they rest in You'
History as the story of God's city, not man's empires
teachers.img: Augustine of Hippo, a North African bishop reading intently in a garden, an open codex of Romans in his hands, tears of relief on his face

q.q: You have made us for Yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in You.
To fall in love with God is the greatest romance; to seek Him the greatest adventure; to find Him, the greatest human achievement.

teachers.sum: This council met to resolve ongoing Trinitarian disputes, officially confirming the full deity of the Holy Spirit against the Pneumatomachians (who denied the Spirit's divinity). By expanding the Nicene Creed, the council established the classic formulation of the Trinity: one God in three co-equal and co-eternal persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). It also condemned Apollinarianism, safeguarding the truth that Christ assumed a fully human mind and soul.
ideas: The Holy Spirit is fully God, proceeding from the Father, and worshiped alongside Father and Son
Classic Trinitarian formulation: one divine essence (ousia) in three distinct persons (hypostases)
Christ took on a complete human nature (body, mind, and soul) to redeem the whole person

Reformed Perspective: Wholeheartedly embraces the expanded Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. However, the Reformed reject the council's political canons elevating the bishop of Constantinople to hierarchical primacy, maintaining that church offices are not divinely ordained hierarchies.
teachers.img: The First Council of Constantinople: A solemn gathering of fourth-century Eastern bishops in a stone basilica, writing and editing the expanded Nicene Creed under flickering candle flames

teachers.sum: Kidnapped to Ireland as a slave boy, Patrick escaped — then returned voluntarily to evangelize his captors' nation. His humble Confession records a mission driven by love and prayer that planted the gospel across Ireland, which in turn sent missionaries back into a collapsing Europe.
ideas: Returning good for evil in mission
The gospel crossing enemy lines
Ordinary weakness carried by God's strength
works: Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus
teachers.img: Patrick of Ireland, a rugged fifth-century missionary bishop with staff preaching to gathered clans on a green Irish hillside

q.q: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me.

teachers.sum: The council resolved the debate between Cyril of Alexandria and Nestorius over the unity of Christ's person. Nestorius was condemned for dividing Christ into two separate persons (one human, one divine), and Mary was affirmed as 'Theotokos' (God-bearer) to emphasize that Jesus is one singular person who is both fully God and fully man from conception. The council also condemned Pelagianism, affirming that humanity cannot take the first step toward salvation without God's grace.
ideas: Jesus Christ is one undivided person, possessing both a divine nature and a human nature
Affirmation of Mary as Theotokos (God-bearer) to safeguard the divine-human unity of Christ's person
Condemnation of Nestorianism and the denial of human ability to save oneself (Pelagianism)

Reformed Perspective: Agrees with the Christological unity and the condemnation of Pelagianism (aligning with sovereign grace). However, Reformed theology strictly warns against the term 'Theotokos' being used to foster mariolatry or prayers to Mary, maintaining that worship belongs solely to God.
teachers.img: The Council of Ephesus: A tense assembly of fifth-century bishops inside the grand, stone-arched Church of Mary in Ephesus, Cyril of Alexandria presenting scrolls as observers listen

teachers.sum: Confronting the Monophysite claim that Christ's human nature was absorbed into his divine nature, the council defined the orthodox understanding of the incarnation. The Chalcedonian Definition declared that Jesus Christ is one person with two distinct natures — fully divine and fully human — united 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.' This permanently shaped Christian Christology, defining Jesus as our perfect mediator.
ideas: Christ is one person (hypostasis) in two distinct natures (physis)
The two natures are united without confusion, without change, without division, without separation
Christ is co-essential (homoousios) with the Father in divinity, and co-essential with us in humanity

Reformed Perspective: Accepted as the high-water mark of biblical Christology, forming the basis of Reformed confessions. The Reformed use the distinction of natures to reject Lutheran ubiquity and Catholic transubstantiation, arguing Christ's human body remains local in heaven.
teachers.img: The Council of Chalcedon: A majestic church council in AD 451, with rows of Eastern and Western bishops in ornate liturgical vestments holding a copy of Leo's Tome and open scrolls of the Gospels

teachers.sum: As Roman order collapsed, Benedict wrote a short, wise Rule for communities of prayer and work ('ora et labora'). Benedictine houses became islands of stability that preserved Scripture, learning, and agriculture through the early Middle Ages — quiet faithfulness that carried civilization.
ideas: Ordered rhythms of prayer, work, and Scripture
Stability and community in chaotic times
Hospitality: receiving every guest as Christ
teachers.img: Benedict of Nursia, a calm abbot in a dark habit on a monastery terrace at Monte Cassino, monks copying manuscripts and tending gardens below

teachers.trad: Bishop of Rome, pastor and reformer
teachers.sum: A Roman administrator who longed for the monastery, Gregory reluctantly became bishop of Rome and defined the office as 'servant of the servants of God.' His Pastoral Rule — how to shepherd different kinds of souls — trained clergy for a millennium, and he sent the mission that evangelized Anglo-Saxon England.
ideas: Leadership as servanthood
Wise, personal care of souls
Mission to unreached peoples
teachers.img: Gregory the Great, a weary but kind bishop of Rome dictating pastoral letters, a dove motif in the lamplit scriptorium behind him

teachers.sum: Called by Emperor Justinian I, the council sought to reconcile the Monophysite churches by condemning the 'Three Chapters' (writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and Ibas of Edessa, who were accused of Nestorian tendencies). The council reaffirmed that the divine Word was personally crucified in the flesh, strengthening the Chalcedonian synthesis and condemning speculative teachings like the pre-existence of souls.
ideas: Reaffirmation of the unity of Christ's person as defined at Chalcedon
Condemnation of the Three Chapters to clarify and defend the true interpretation of Chalcedon
Condemnation of speculative doctrines, including the pre-existence and ultimate restoration of all souls

Reformed Perspective: Accepts the Christological unity affirmed here, but views the council as a warning against excessive imperial interference in church doctrine (Caesaropapism) and the fallibility of ecclesiastical assemblies.
teachers.img: The Second Council of Constantinople: Emperor Justinian I sitting on an imperial throne overlooking a circle of bishops debating theology in a grand Byzantine palace hall

teachers.sum: Writing from a monastery under early Islamic rule, John distilled seven centuries of Greek theology into a single ordered summary, The Orthodox Faith — a bridge over which the Fathers' teaching passed to both East and West. His hymns are still sung at Easter in Eastern churches.
ideas: Faithful summary of the Fathers' consensus
Theology preserved under foreign rule
Doctrine sung: hymns as teaching
works: The Fountain of Knowledge (incl. The Orthodox Faith)
teachers.img: John of Damascus, an eighth-century monk writing in a cliff-side desert monastery near Jerusalem, ordered rows of Greek volumes beside him

teachers.sum: This council addressed the Monothelite controversy, which suggested that Christ had two natures but only one divine will. The council decided that Christ possesses two natural wills (one divine, one human) and two natural operations, corresponding to his two natures. His human will was perfectly obedient and subordinate to his divine will. Crucially, the council condemned Pope Honorius I for his monothelite views, confirming that even popes are subject to heresy.
ideas: Jesus Christ has two natural wills (divine and human) and two natural operations
Christ's human will is perfectly aligned with and subordinate to his divine will, never in conflict
Condemnation of Pope Honorius I, showing that church leadership is subject to error and theological judgment

Reformed Perspective: Fully accepts the theological decision as essential to Christ's true humanity and mediator role. The condemnation of Pope Honorius is frequently cited by Reformers to refute the Roman Catholic dogma of papal infallibility.
teachers.img: The Third Council of Constantinople: A large Byzantine assembly of bishops in AD 680, examining letters and texts from both East and West, with an empty throne representing Christ's presence at the center of the hall

teachers.sum: The council resolved the fierce Iconoclastic controversy by restoring the use and veneration of icons. It drew a sharp theological distinction between 'latria' (the adoration and worship due to God alone) and 'proskynesis' or 'dulia' (the honor and veneration given to icons, saints, and angels as windows to the divine). This decision permanently defined the role of images and physical art in Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic worship.
ideas: Restoration of icons and images of Christ, Mary, and the saints to churches
Theological distinction: worship (latria) is for God alone; honor (proskynesis/dulia) is for icons/saints
Affirmation of the goodness of matter, arguing that the Incarnation sanctified the physical world

Reformed Perspective: Strongly rejected. Reformed theology views the veneration of icons as a violation of the Second Commandment, dismissing the distinction between latria and dulia as practically meaningless, and holds to the Regulative Principle of Worship.
works: Decree of the Second Council of Nicaea
teachers.img: The Second Council of Nicaea: Empress Irene and early bishops in a grand basilica, surrounded by newly restored, colorful Christian icons, debating theological distinctions between worship and veneration

teachers.sum: Anselm prayed his theology, defining it as 'faith seeking understanding.' In Why God Became Man he argued that sin is a debt to God's honor so great that only one who is both God and man could pay it — the classic statement of why the incarnation and the cross belong together.
ideas: Faith seeking understanding
The cross as satisfaction of sin's debt
Only the God-man can save
works: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)
teachers.img: Anselm of Canterbury, a gentle Norman-era archbishop praying over an open manuscript in a candlelit abbey chapter house

q.q: I do not seek to understand that I may believe, but I believe in order to understand.

teachers.trad: Abbot, teacher of the love of God
teachers.sum: The most influential churchman of his century, Bernard taught that the Christian life is a growing love for God for God's own sake. His sermons on the Song of Songs and hymns of devotion to Jesus ('Jesus, the very thought of Thee') fed centuries of believers — the Reformers later quoted him constantly on grace.
ideas: Loving God for Himself, not His gifts
Warm, Christ-centered devotion
Grace cherished within medieval faith
works: Sermons on the Song of Songs
teachers.img: Bernard of Clairvaux, a thin white-robed Cistercian abbot preaching to monks in a bare stone abbey, morning light through plain glass

q.q: Jesus, the very thought of Thee with sweetness fills the breast.

teachers.sum: The rich merchant's son who embraced radical poverty, Francis took Jesus' sending of the disciples literally — preaching, serving lepers, owning nothing. His joyful simplicity and love for all God's creation rebuked a wealthy church and still challenges comfortable Christianity.
ideas: Radical simplicity for the sake of the gospel
Joy and gratitude in creation as God's gift
Serving the poorest as serving Christ
teachers.img: Francis of Assisi, a joyful ragged friar in a patched brown habit among lepers and birds outside Assisi's walls, Umbrian hills behind

teachers.sum: The great systematizer of medieval theology, Thomas ordered the whole of Christian doctrine in his Summa Theologiae, showing that faith and reason are allies because all truth is God's truth. Near the end of his life a profound experience of God left him calling his massive work 'straw' beside the reality itself.
ideas: Faith and reason in harmony
All truth is God's truth
Ordered, careful doctrinal thinking
Knowing about God is not yet knowing God
teachers.img: Thomas Aquinas, a large quiet Dominican friar in black and white habit at a manuscript-covered desk in a Paris university hall

q.q: To one who has faith, no explanation is necessary. To one without faith, no explanation is possible.

teachers.sum: An Oxford scholar a century and a half before Luther, Wycliffe taught that Scripture is the supreme authority over popes and councils and sponsored the first complete English Bible. His traveling preachers carried the Scriptures to ordinary people, and his ideas — condemned in his lifetime — kindled fires he never saw.
ideas: Scripture over every human authority
The Bible belongs in the people's language
Reform seeded a century before the Reformation
works: On the Truth of Holy Scripture
teachers.img: John Wycliffe, a stern Oxford scholar in a fur-trimmed academic gown handing a hand-copied English Bible to plainly dressed traveling preachers

teachers.sum: A Prague preacher who took up Wycliffe's ideas, Hus preached in Czech against clerical corruption and for Christ as the true head of the church. Promised safe conduct to the Council of Constance, he was burned anyway — reportedly saying they might cook his goose ('Hus'), but a swan would rise after him. Luther later saw himself in that word.
ideas: Christ, not any human office, is head of the church
Preaching in the people's language
Costly integrity: truth over safety
teachers.img: Jan Hus, a resolute Czech preacher at the stake in Constance, praying aloud as the fire is lit, dignitaries watching uneasily

teachers.sum: A quiet monk who spent seventy years copying Scripture and writing, Thomas produced The Imitation of Christ — after the Bible, perhaps the most widely read Christian book in history. Its call to humble, inward devotion to Jesus over outward show has steadied believers of every tradition.
ideas: Inward devotion over outward religion
Humility as the path of discipleship
Daily imitation of Christ's life
teachers.img: Thomas à Kempis, a peaceful elderly monk copying Scripture by candlelight in a small Dutch monastery cell, snow at the window

q.q: Without the Way, there is no going; without the Truth, there is no knowing; without the Life, there is no living.

teachers.sum: Defying a ban, Tyndale translated the New Testament from Greek into vivid English and smuggled it into England in bales of cloth, vowing that a plow-boy would know more Scripture than the clergy. Strangled and burned in 1536, his dying prayer — 'Lord, open the king of England's eyes' — was answered within years; some nine-tenths of the King James New Testament is his wording.
ideas: The Bible in the common tongue at any cost
Translation from the original languages
The English Bible's founding voice
works: The Obedience of a Christian Man
teachers.img: William Tyndale, a hunted scholar translating by candlelight in an Antwerp attic room, Greek text open, printed pages hidden in cloth bales

q.q: If God spare my life, ere many years I will cause a boy that driveth the plough shall know more of the Scripture than thou dost.
q.src: to a clergyman, as reported by Foxe

teachers.sum: An anguished monk who found peace in Romans 1:17 — the righteous shall live by faith — Luther ignited the Reformation with his Ninety-five Theses in 1517. He recovered the gospel of justification by faith alone, translated the Bible into German, put hymnbooks in congregations' hands, and taught that every believer stands as a priest before God.
ideas: Justification by faith alone
Scripture alone as final authority
The priesthood of all believers
Worship and Scripture in the people's language
teachers.img: Martin Luther, a sturdy German monk in an Augustinian habit nailing a parchment of theses to a heavy wooden church door in Wittenberg

q.q: My conscience is captive to the Word of God... Here I stand, I can do no other. God help me. Amen.
We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.

teachers.sum: Independently of Luther, Zwingli began expository preaching straight through Matthew in Zurich in 1519 — verse by verse, book by book — and reformed the city by the Word alone. His insistence that worship and practice be grounded in Scripture shaped the Reformed tradition's whole approach to church life.
ideas: Consecutive expository preaching through books
Worship governed by Scripture
Civic life reformed by the Word
works: Commentary on True and False Religion
teachers.img: Ulrich Zwingli, a Swiss reformer preaching from an open Bible in Zurich's Grossmünster, no images on the whitewashed walls, burghers listening

teachers.sum: A shy French scholar conscripted into leading Geneva's reform, Calvin gave Protestantism its most complete theology in the Institutes of the Christian Religion and commentaries on nearly the whole Bible. His vision of God's sovereign grace in salvation, and of all of life — work, family, government — lived 'coram Deo' (before the face of God), shaped churches and cultures worldwide.
ideas: God's sovereignty in salvation and all of life
Scripture self-authenticating by the Spirit's witness
Every vocation lived before the face of God
Doctrine ordered for the church, not the academy
works: Commentaries on most of the Bible
teachers.img: John Calvin, a slight bearded French scholar in a plain black robe and cap, lecturing from Scripture in a candlelit Geneva auditorium

q.q: My heart I offer to you, Lord, promptly and sincerely.

teachers.trad: Archbishop, liturgist of the English Reformation
teachers.sum: Architect of the English Reformation, Cranmer gave the English-speaking church the Book of Common Prayer — Scripture-saturated worship in language of enduring beauty. Forced under Mary to recant, he publicly withdrew the recantation at his burning and thrust the offending hand that signed it into the flames first.
ideas: Common worship shaped by Scripture
Prayers the people can pray and understand
Repentance and courage at the last
teachers.img: Thomas Cranmer, an aged archbishop at the stake in Oxford, deliberately extending his right hand into the flames

teachers.sum: A Dutch priest converted through studying Scripture, Menno gathered the scattered, persecuted Anabaptists into disciplined communities marked by believer's baptism, nonviolence, and visible discipleship. The Mennonites who bear his name carried forward the conviction that the church is a community of committed believers, not an arm of the state.
ideas: Believer's baptism upon confession of faith
The church as a voluntary, visible community
Peace and nonresistance as discipleship
teachers.img: Menno Simons, a careful Dutch pastor teaching a small congregation gathered quietly in a candlelit barn, a Bible open on a plain table

teachers.sum: Galley slave, exile, and finally preacher who reformed a nation, Knox brought Geneva's fire to Scotland and stood fearlessly before queens — praying, it was said, 'Give me Scotland, or I die.' The Presbyterian pattern of church life and the Scots' passion for an educated, Bible-reading people trace to him.
ideas: Fearless preaching to power
A church ordered by elders, not prelates
A school beside every church: universal Bible literacy
works: History of the Reformation in Scotland
teachers.img: John Knox, a fierce grey-bearded Scottish preacher thundering from a high wooden pulpit at St Giles, Edinburgh

q.q: A man with God is always in the majority.

teachers.sum: A tinker turned preacher who spent twelve years in Bedford jail rather than stop preaching, Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress there — the allegory of Christian's journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City that became, after the Bible, the most printed book in English. Generations learned the shape of the Christian life from it.
ideas: The Christian life as pilgrimage
Conscience bound to God over the law of man
Plain, vivid gospel storytelling for ordinary people
works: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
teachers.img: John Bunyan, a broad-shouldered English preacher writing at a small table in a dim Bedford jail cell, pilgrim's pack and scroll sketched on pages around him

q.q: As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a den, and laid me down in that place to sleep; and as I slept, I dreamed a dream.

teachers.sum: The deepest of the Puritan theologians, Owen wrote with surgical care on the glory of Christ, the work of the Spirit, and the daily war against indwelling sin — 'be killing sin or it will be killing you.' His treatises remain the classic guide to fighting sin by the Spirit rather than by willpower.
ideas: Mortification: putting sin to death by the Spirit
Communion with each person of the Trinity
The glory of Christ as the believer's food
works: The Death of Death in the Death of Christ
teachers.img: John Owen, a grave Puritan divine in black with white collar, writing among towering stacks of theology in an Oxford study

q.q: Be killing sin or it will be killing you.

teachers.sum: Baxter turned the rough town of Kidderminster upside down by systematic personal shepherding — catechizing every family, house by house, year after year. The Reformed Pastor, his charge to ministers ('take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock'), remains the standard for pastoral care; his Saints' Everlasting Rest taught believers to live heavenward.
ideas: Personal, house-to-house pastoral care
The pastor's own soul as his first charge
Living daily in view of eternal rest
teachers.img: Richard Baxter, an earnest Puritan pastor seated at a cottage table catechizing a weaver's family, loom in the corner, Bible open between them

q.q: I preached as never sure to preach again, and as a dying man to dying men.

teachers.sum: America's greatest theologian, Edwards preached at the center of the Great Awakening and then analyzed it with rare honesty in Religious Affections — true faith shows itself not in emotional heat alone but in a changed heart that loves God's beauty. His vision of God's glory as the end of all things still sets the horizon for many.
ideas: True religion as new affections, not bare emotion
The beauty and sweetness of God's holiness
Revival tested by lasting fruit
God's glory as the purpose of everything
works: The End for Which God Created the World
Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God (sermon)
teachers.img: Jonathan Edwards, a lean colonial minister in black reading a sermon manuscript by candlelight in a plain New England meetinghouse

q.q: Resolved: that all men should live for the glory of God. Resolved second: that whether others do or not, I will.

teachers.sum: After his heart was 'strangely warmed' at Aldersgate, Wesley rode a quarter-million miles preaching in fields, prisons, and pit-heads to people the churches never reached, organizing converts into small accountability groups — the original small-group discipleship. With his brother Charles's hymns, Methodism carried holiness of heart and life across the English-speaking world.
ideas: Small groups for discipleship and accountability
Taking the gospel outside church walls
Holiness of heart and life
Faith working through organized love for the poor
works: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament
teachers.img: John Wesley, a small tireless preacher in clerical black preaching from horseback to a crowd of miners at dawn outside a coal pit

q.q: I look upon all the world as my parish.

teachers.sum: The most heard preacher of his century, Whitefield crossed the Atlantic thirteen times and preached perhaps eighteen thousand sermons to open-air crowds in the tens of thousands, voice carrying like a trumpet: 'You must be born again.' His itinerant field-preaching made the new birth the heartbeat of evangelicalism.
ideas: The necessity of the new birth
Open-air evangelism to the masses
Gospel partnership across denominational lines
teachers.img: George Whitefield, a robed evangelist preaching from a wooden platform to an immense open field crowd, arms outstretched, stormy light breaking through

q.q: I am content to wait till the day of judgment for the clearing up of my reputation; and after I am dead I desire no other epitaph than this, "Here lies G.W. What sort of man he was the great day will discover."

teachers.sum: A poor cobbler with a homemade world map, Carey shattered the complacency of his day — 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God' — and sailed for India, where he translated the Bible into dozens of languages and fought social evils. The modern missionary movement traces its rise to him.
ideas: The Great Commission binding on every generation
Bible translation at the heart of mission
Long obedience: decades of unglamorous labor
works: An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians
Bengali Bible and many other translations
teachers.img: William Carey, a plain Englishman at a Serampore desk crowded with type trays and manuscripts in Bengali and Sanskrit, Indian pundits working alongside

q.q: Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.

teachers.sum: Converted as a teenager in a snowstorm-emptied chapel, Spurgeon was preaching to thousands in London by twenty. For nearly four decades at the Metropolitan Tabernacle he preached Christ from every text — his printed sermons sold in the tens of millions — while founding a pastors' college, orphanages, and dozens of ministries, all through long seasons of depression he spoke of openly.
ideas: Christ at the center of every sermon
Plain speech that ordinary people love
Word and deed: orphanages beside the pulpit
Honesty about suffering and depression in ministry
teachers.img: Charles Spurgeon, a stout Victorian preacher gripping the rail of the vast Metropolitan Tabernacle platform, thousands of faces rising tier on tier

q.q: I have learned to kiss the wave that throws me against the Rock of Ages.
Visit many good books, but live in the Bible.

teachers.sum: Taylor founded the China Inland Mission on radical trust — no appeals for funds, workers dressed in Chinese clothes, headquarters in China itself — to carry the gospel beyond the port cities into every inland province. His identification with the people he served reset the standard for cross-cultural mission.
ideas: Cultural identification: becoming like those you reach
Faith missions: God's work, done God's way, will not lack supply
Pressing to the unreached interior
teachers.img: Hudson Taylor, an English missionary in Chinese scholar's dress and queue, teaching from an open Bible in an inland Chinese courtyard

q.q: God's work done in God's way will never lack God's supply.

teachers.sum: A brilliant young theologian who led the Confessing Church's resistance to Hitler's takeover of German Christianity, Bonhoeffer warned against 'cheap grace' — forgiveness without repentance, discipleship without the cross. Hanged in a concentration camp weeks before liberation, his life sealed his book's claim: 'When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.'
ideas: Costly grace versus cheap grace
The church must not bow to ideology
Discipleship as concrete obedience
Life together: Christian community under the Word
teachers.img: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a young German pastor in round glasses leading secret seminary students in prayer around a farmhouse table, 1930s Germany

q.q: When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.

teachers.sum: An Oxford don and reluctant convert — 'the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England' — Lewis became the twentieth century's most read defender of 'mere Christianity,' the core convictions shared across the traditions. Through logic in Mere Christianity and imagination in Narnia and The Screwtape Letters, he made the faith intelligible and desirable to millions.
ideas: Mere Christianity: the great common core of the faith
Imagination as a road to truth
Joy and longing as signposts to God
Plain-language apologetics for ordinary readers
teachers.img: C. S. Lewis, a tweed-jacketed Oxford don with pipe and pint at a worn pub table, notebooks and letters spread before the fire

q.q: I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen: not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.

teachers.trad: Pastor and writer on the knowledge of God
teachers.sum: A self-educated Chicago pastor, Tozer diagnosed the modern church's shallowness at its root: a too-small view of God. The Knowledge of the Holy and The Pursuit of God called believers back to worship — 'What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.'
ideas: Recovering a high, holy view of God
Worship as the church's first calling
Hunger for God over religious routine
teachers.img: A. W. Tozer, a spare mid-century American pastor kneeling in prayer over an open Bible in a bare study, city light through blinds

q.q: What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.

teachers.sum: From a North Carolina dairy farm to stadiums on every continent, Graham preached the gospel in person to more people than anyone in history — always the same simple message, 'the Bible says,' and the same invitation to come to Christ. His integrity in finances and conduct across seventy years gave modern evangelism its trusted model.
ideas: Simple, direct gospel invitation
'The Bible says': authority in preaching
Integrity structures guarding a long ministry
Cooperation across churches for evangelism
teachers.img: Billy Graham, a tall evangelist with an open Bible in one hand preaching in a packed floodlit stadium at night, crowds streaming forward

q.q: My home is in Heaven. I'm just traveling through this world.

teachers.trad: Baptismal confession of the Western church
teachers.sum: The oldest and simplest summary of the Christian faith, grown from the baptismal confessions of the early Roman church. In a few lines it walks through Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — creation, the story of Jesus from conception to return, and the church's shared hope. Not written by the apostles themselves, but so called because it summarizes their teaching.
ideas: God the Father, maker of heaven and earth
The true story of Jesus: born, crucified, risen, returning
The Holy Spirit, the church, forgiveness, resurrection

teachers.trad: The ecumenical confession of the deity of Christ
teachers.sum: Forged at the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) against teachers who made the Son a creature, this creed confesses Jesus Christ as 'true God from true God, begotten not made, of one being with the Father.' It remains the one confession shared by nearly every Christian tradition on earth.
ideas: The Son is of one being (homoousios) with the Father
The Holy Spirit is Lord and giver of life, worshiped with Father and Son
One baptism for the forgiveness of sins

teachers.trad: The classic statement of Christ as one person in two natures
teachers.sum: The council of Chalcedon's answer to a century of confusion about how Jesus can be both God and man: one person in two natures, 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.' Fully God, fully man, one Christ — the guardrails inside which all faithful talk about Jesus still runs.
ideas: One person, two natures — truly God and truly man
The natures are neither blended nor separated
Mary is rightly called God-bearer (Theotokos) because her son is God the Son

teachers.sum: A warm, pastoral question-and-answer summary of the faith, written for churches and schools of the Palatinate. Its famous first question sets the tone: 'What is your only comfort in life and in death? That I am not my own, but belong — body and soul, in life and in death — to my faithful Savior, Jesus Christ.'
ideas: Guilt, grace, gratitude — the shape of the Christian life
Comfort rooted in belonging to Christ
The catechism as a tool for teaching households the faith

teachers.trad: The definitive Reformed confession in English
teachers.sum: Drawn up by the Westminster Assembly during the English civil war, this confession became the doctrinal standard of Presbyterian churches worldwide. It opens not with God but with Scripture — the rule by which everything else is measured — and its Shorter Catechism taught generations that 'man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.'
ideas: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life
God's sovereign covenant of grace
Man's chief end: to glorify God and enjoy Him forever

teachers.trad: The historic confession of Particular Baptist churches
teachers.sum: When toleration finally came to England, the Particular Baptists published the confession their churches had quietly shared for years — deliberately tracking the Westminster Confession to show their unity with Reformed Christians, while confessing believer's baptism and the local church gathered by covenant. It remains the doctrinal root of many Baptist churches today.
ideas: Believer's baptism by immersion
The gathered local church under Christ its head
Reformed doctrine held in Baptist form
